ap_physics_1-f01.title: Elevator motion in three stages: v-t graph and scale reading

stimulus.description: A person of mass $m=60\text{ kg}$ stands on a scale in an elevator that moves upward along a vertical shaft. Starting from rest, the elevator speeds up uniformly with acceleration $a_1=1.5\text{ m/s}^2$ for $t_1=2\text{ s}$, then moves at constant velocity for $t_2=5\text{ s}$, and then slows down uniformly to a stop in $t_3=4\text{ s}$. The scale reads the magnitude of the normal force on the person. Blank axes for the graphs are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the velocity $v$ of the elevator as a function of time $t$ for the whole trip. Label the axes with quantities and units and label the key values of velocity and time.
parts.model_answer: A straight line from the origin up to $v=3.00\text{ m/s}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$, a horizontal line at that velocity until $t=7\text{ s}$, and a straight line down to zero at $t=11\text{ s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units and a scale is shown
common_errors: omits units

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line from the origin rising to about $3.00\text{ m/s}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$
common_errors: draws a curve instead of a straight line for uniform acceleration

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a horizontal segment at the same velocity from $t=2\text{ s}$ to $t=7\text{ s}$
common_errors: draws the constant-velocity segment with a slope

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line down to zero velocity at $t=11\text{ s}$
common_errors: ends the graph below zero velocity

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the total distance that the elevator rises during the whole trip. Show how you use your graph from part A.
parts.model_answer: The displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph: $y=\tfrac12(3.00)(2)+(3.00)(5)+\tfrac12(3.00)(4)\approx 24.0\text{ m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the displacement as the area under the velocity-time graph
required_elements: displacement is the area under the v-t graph
common_errors: uses the slope of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Adds the areas of the triangle, the rectangle, and the second triangle: $\tfrac12vt_1+vt_2+\tfrac12vt_3$
common_errors: omits one of the three areas

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a total distance of about 24.0 with units of meters
common_errors: uses the average velocity of only the first segment

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the reading of the scale (the magnitude of the normal force on the person) during the first stage, when the elevator is speeding up. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Newton's second law gives $N-mg=ma_1$, so $N=m(g+a_1)=(60)(9.8+1.5)\approx 678\text{ N}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to the person with the normal force up and the weight down: $N-mg=ma_1$
common_errors: uses N = m g
subtracts the acceleration term

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for the normal force: $N=m(g+a_1)$
common_errors: gets $N=m(g-a_1)$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a reading of about 678 with units of newtons
common_errors: uses a mass in the units of newtons

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: In a second trip the constant-velocity stage is made $4\text{ s}$ longer while everything else about the trip is unchanged. By how much does the total distance that the elevator rises change? Justify your answer using your velocity-time graph from part A.
parts.model_answer: The distance increases by $v\Delta t=3.00\times4=12.0\text{ m}$, because the added area under the graph is a rectangle of height $v=3.00\text{ m/s}$ and width $4\text{ s}$ and the other two areas do not change.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the distance increases by about 12.0 with units of meters
common_errors: states the distance does not change because the velocity is constant

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the extra area under the graph is a rectangle of height equal to the constant velocity, with the other areas unchanged
required_elements: added rectangle of height v and width delta t
common_errors: argues only that the elevator travels longer

ap_physics_1-f02.title: Two satellites in circular orbits

stimulus.description: Two satellites orbit Earth in circular orbits. Satellite 1 has an orbital radius of $r_1=8e+06\text{ m}$ (measured from the center of Earth) and satellite 2 has an orbital radius of $r_2=1.6e+07\text{ m}$, which is $2$ times as great. The mass of Earth is $M$. Treat Earth as a uniform sphere.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that satellite 2 has a smaller orbital speed than satellite 1. Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer using Newton's law of gravitation and the condition for circular motion.
parts.model_answer: Agree. The gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$, so $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ and the speed decreases as the radius increases.

rubric_rows.criterion: Agrees that the speed of satellite 2 is smaller
common_errors: disagrees because a farther satellite must move faster

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by setting the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$
required_elements: G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r
common_errors: uses the weight mg at the surface of Earth for every orbit

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the reason that $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$, so the speed decreases as the radius increases
common_errors: concludes that the speed is independent of the radius

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the orbital speed $v$ of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ in terms of $M$, $r$, and fundamental constants, and then determine the numerical ratio $v_2/v_1$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ from $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$
common_errors: leaves the mass of the satellite in the expression

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the ratio $v_2/v_1=\sqrt{r_1/r_2}$
common_errors: inverts the ratio under the square root

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $v_2/v_1\approx 0.707$ (no units)
common_errors: uses the ratio of the radii without the square root

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Satellite 2 is $2$ times as far from the center of Earth as satellite 1. Predict the ratio of the period of satellite 2 to the period of satellite 1. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The period is $T=2\pi r/v=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}$, so $T_2/T_1=(2)^{3/2}=2.83$: the period of satellite 2 is about 2.8 times as long.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the ratio of the periods is about 2.8 (the period of satellite 2 is greater)
common_errors: states that the periods are equal
uses the ratio of the radii

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $T=2\pi r/v$ and $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$, which gives $T\propto r^{3/2}$
required_elements: T proportional to r to the 3/2
common_errors: argues only that a larger orbit takes more time

ap_physics_1-f03.title: Experiment: gravitational field strength from a cart on a tilted track

stimulus.description: A student releases a low-friction cart from rest on a track that is tilted at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and measures the acceleration of the cart down the track with a motion sensor. The student repeats the experiment for several angles and wants to determine the gravitational field strength $g$.

notes: A student releases a low-friction cart from rest on a track that is tilted at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and measures the acceleration of the cart down the track with a motion sensor. The student repeats the experiment for several angles and wants to determine the gravitational field strength $g$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the acceleration as a function of the angle. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the measured angle.
parts.model_answer: Use a protractor (or measure the height of the raised end and the length of the track and find the angle from a trigonometric ratio) to set each angle of the track and a motion sensor to measure the acceleration; change only the angle with the same cart and track; reduce the uncertainty in the angle by measuring the height and the length with a meterstick and calculating the angle.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a way to set and measure the angle and a way to measure the acceleration (motion sensor or a time and distance measurement)
required_elements: a way to measure the angle and a way to measure the acceleration
common_errors: omits how the acceleration is measured

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the angle while using the same cart and the same track (both conditions are needed)
required_elements: change only the angle with the same cart and track

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces the uncertainty in the angle by calculating it from the height and the length measured with a meterstick, or by repeating the measurement and averaging (either earns the point)
required_elements: calculate the angle from the height and the length or repeat and average (either earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using the relationship between the acceleration of the cart, the angle of the track, and $g$ when friction is negligible, identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to find $g$.
parts.model_answer: For a frictionless incline $a=g\sin\theta$: plot $a$ on the vertical axis against $\sin\theta$ on the horizontal axis; the slope is $g$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $a$ (vertical) versus $\sin\theta$ (horizontal)
common_errors: plots a versus theta

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data in a form that gives a straight line, and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units (sin theta has no units) and the scale fills most of the grid
common_errors: scale uses less than half the grid

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the five points $(\sin\theta, a)$ accurately
Draws a straight best-fit line through the trend of the points
common_errors: connects the dots

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Use the best-fit line to determine the gravitational field strength $g$. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: The slope of the best-fit line is $g\approx 9.7\text{ m/s}^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the slope of the best-fit line using two points on the line (about 9.69 m/s^2; accept any value within 5 percent)
common_errors: uses data points rather than points on the line

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates the slope to the gravitational field strength: slope $=g$
common_errors: uses slope = 1/g

rubric_rows.criterion: States $g$ (about 9.7; accept any value within 8 percent) with units of meters per second squared or newtons per kilogram
alt_solutions: a value of g consistent with the student's own slope from D1
